detail.abstract: Using various machine learning and standard accounting- and market-based financial ratios, we predict corporate default across different time horizons. We find similar specificity and recall metrics across all methodologies, with XGBoost slightly outperforming the rest of the methods. Contrary to Logistic Regression the rest of the methodologies in this paper identify small subsets of ratios as important for predicting default, e.g., Debt Ratio, Interest Coverage, Price-to-Earnings, and Net Profit. We observe a decoupling between financial ratios that are significant out-of-sample default predictors according to the machine learning algorithms and those that are included in debt covenants or that can explain the cost of debt in-sample. These findings suggest that creditors should update their baseline approach to writing debt contracts, i.e., specifying interest rates and debt covenants that monitor financial ratios, by incorporating information from financial ratios that are important out-of-sample default predictors according to machine learning approaches.

title: When Swords Need Words: Military Unification and Pro-religion Rule
affiliations: Fudan University - Department of Economics, Fudan University and Renmin University of China

detail.title: When Swords Need Words: Military Unification and Pro-religion Rule
detail.abstract: During the 1,500 years before the Industrial Revolution, Eurasia witnessed divergent religious trajectories: Western Europe developed independent religious authority, while China maintained state-dominated religion. We propose that fragmentation-driven warfare prompts rulers to promote religion for legitimacy. Evidence from Imperial China demonstrates that emperors pursuing military unification were significantly more likely to adopt pro-religion policies, with legitimacy-deficient rulers showing particularly strong adoption of this strategy. These findings provide suggestive evidence that Europe's prolonged polycentrism fostered stronger religious institutions, offering a new perspective on the East-West Great Divergence.

title: How does an active secondary stock market enhance total factor productivity of non-listed enterprises? Evidence from China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How does an active secondary stock market enhance total factor productivity of non-listed enterprises? Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the stock market can enhance the total factor productivity (TFP) of non-listed enterprises. We propose that increased stock liquidity of listed companies promotes TFP growth in non-listed enterprises through three channels: (i) an information mechanism, by facilitating learning from investors' assessments of leading innovations; (ii) a financing mechanism, by mitigating financing constraint effects; and (iii) a governance mechanism, by alleviating principal-agent conflicts. These channels enhance the decision-making capabilities of non-listed enterprises, enabling them to better follow leading innovations and develop complementary technologies. Consequently, this mitigates innovation imbalance within the industry and ultimately boosts TFP growth. Empirical results corroborate the information and governance channels, but not the financing channel. This study provides evidence that the stock market generates positive externalities for the productivity growth of non-listed enterprises.

title: Scenario dynamics of degrowth under capitalist power
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Scenario dynamics of degrowth under capitalist power
detail.abstract: This article develops a framework for analyzing degrowth futures through the lens of Capital as Power (CasP). It translates CasP’s account of accumulation—organized through capitalization, sabotage, and state–capital entanglement—into a causal loop architecture. This approach clarifies how degrowth transformations interact with capitalist power through distinct feedback dynamics. Four scenarios are examined: (1) sabotaged transition, where degrowth initiatives are redirected to sustain accumulation; (2) post-growth accumulation, where reduced aggregate growth remains compatible with scarcity-based profits; (3) contested transformation, where degrowth confronts capital and sparks escalating conflict; and (4) systemic reordering, where confidence in capitalization unravels and capitalist order destabilizes. The analysis shows that reduced growth does not automatically weaken dominant capital, as stagnation and scarcity can sustain differential accumulation. For degrowth, this highlights that futures must be conceived as transformations of power relations: constraining the routes through which dominant capital increases its relative power, undermining the restrictions imposed on alternatives, and challenging the confidence capitalists have in the continuity of the order they rule. Degrowth futures must therefore be understood as struggles over the enforcement or destabilization of capitalist power.

title: Does Law Codification Bring the Disadvantaged into the Legal System?
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: Does Law Codification Bring the Disadvantaged into the Legal System?
detail.abstract: Does the codification of law lead disadvantaged groups to make more use of the legal system? I address this question by studying a natural experiment in Prussia. In 1794, King Frederick sought to empower the masses by harmonizing society’s many rules, orders, and laws into a clean legal code, which could be understood by all citizens. Using archival sentencing data, I show that codification led underrepresented groups to sue more frequently and to focus their lawsuits on issues closely linked to their preferences. In particular, women and non-aristocrats became more likely to sue on economic and family-related grounds, respectively. Women also became more likely to win in court. To explain this finding, I show that codification made sentences both more concise and easier to understand, thus opening the legal system to the disadvantaged.

title: The costs of social and environmental degradation in affluent economies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and STATEC

detail.title: The costs of social and environmental degradation in affluent economies
detail.abstract: Individuals’ attempts to defend from the deterioration of common goods, such as natural and social capital, stimulate defensive growth, that is new economic activity driven by private solutions to collective problems. We use a compensating differential approach to compute the monetary valuation of social and environmental degradation, and provide an estimate of defensive expenditures - the individual consumption needed to protect against the decay of common goods.  To do so, we conduct a regression analysis of life satisfaction on aggregate consumption levels and various social and environmental externalities (which we refer to as "bads"). Our findings indicate that the consumption needed to defend against collective problems is worth nearly a quarter of observed consumption, and nearly half Gross Domestic Product per capita in affluent economies. Defensive consumption stimulates economic growth, however, in so far as the equivalent of nearly half of such growth is defensive, its expansion does not reflect true progress.

title: Greener Under Pressure? The Local Geography of Import Competition and Emissions in Swedish Manufacturing
affiliations: Lund University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Greener Under Pressure? The Local Geography of Import Competition and Emissions in Swedish Manufacturing
detail.abstract: We examine how local import competition — measured across different spatial dimensions within Sweden — affects the CO2 emission intensity of manufacturing firms in Sweden. Leveraging detailed geographic data on the location of all Swedish manufacturing firms, we provide evidence that increased local import competition leads to lower emissions at the firm level, with the effect diminishing as the distance between producers and importers increases. Our findings indicate that relying on national-level measures of import competition may significantly underestimate the true environmental impact of trade shocks. We identify two primary mechanisms behind these reductions: (i) a pro-competitive efficiency-enhancing effect, where firms experience gains in total factor productivity, increasing value-added, lower marginal costs, and higher markups; and (ii) a product-mix effect, where firms reallocate production away from emission-intensive goods toward cleaner alternatives. Additionally, we find some evidence of firms relying on carbon offshoring as a response to import competition, as well as reliance on investment in pollution abatement, suggesting that firms adopt a mix of strategies to deal with increasing import competition.

title: Fuzzy Clustering of EU Countries within the Doughnut Economics Framework: Social and Environmental Boundaries
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Institute of Economics, Zagreb

detail.title: Fuzzy Clustering of EU Countries within the Doughnut Economics Framework: Social and Environmental Boundaries
detail.abstract: This study assesses the position of EU-27 countries within the Safe and Just Space (SJS) of the Doughnut Economics (DE) framework by integrating Ecological Distance Index (EDI) and Social Distance Index (SDI) metrics with fuzzy c-means clustering. 13 environmental and 28 social indicators, benchmarked against normative thresholds, quantify overshoots of planetary boundaries and shortfalls from social foundations. Distances are expressed as percentages of thresholds, enabling consistent interpretation across indicators. Fuzzy clustering identifies five environmental and six social typologies, revealing structural similarities that often transcend geography. No Member State lies within the SJS: high social performance frequently coincides with ecological overshoot, while lower overshoot tends to align with weaker social outcomes. The most common transgressions relate to greenhouse gas emissions, biochemical flows, and income inequality. Transitional cases, identified through fuzzy memberships, highlight countries shifting between sustainability profiles. Findings stress the need for cluster-specific policy strategies -from reducing resource footprints to targeted equity measures and for peer learning among countries facing similar challenges.

title: Virtue or Mirage? Complexity in Exchange Rate Prediction
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Virtue or Mirage? Complexity in Exchange Rate Prediction

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the “virtue of complexity” (VoC), documented in equity return prediction, extends to exchange rate forecasting. Using nonlinear Ridge regressions with Random Fourier Features (Ridge–RFF), we compare the predictive performance of complex models against linear regression and the robust random walk benchmark. Forecasts are constructed across three sets of economic fundamentals—traditional monetary, expanded monetary and non-monetary, and Taylor-rule predictors—with nominal complexity varied through rolling training windows of 12, 60, and 120 months. Our results offer a cautionary perspective. Complexity delivers only modest, localized gains: in very small samples with rich predictor sets, Ridge–RFF can outperform linear regression. Yet these improvements never translate into systematic gains over the random walk. As training windows expand, Ridge–RFF quickly loses ground, while linear regression increasingly dominates, at times even surpassing the random walk under expanded fundamentals. Market-timing analyses reinforce these findings: complexity-based strategies yield occasional short-sample gains but are unstable and prone to sharp drawdowns, whereas simpler linear and random walk strategies provide more robust and consistent economic value. By incorporating formal forecast evaluation tests—including Clark–West and Diebold–Mariano—we show that apparent gains from complexity are fragile and rarely statistically significant. Overall, our evidence points to a limited virtue of complexity in FX forecasting: complexity may help under narrowly defined conditions, but parsimony and the random walk benchmark remain more reliable across samples, predictor sets, and economic evaluations.

title: Racial Differences in Nursing Home Value Added

detail.title: Racial Differences in Nursing Home Value Added

detail.abstract: We use detailed data on the evolution of health for about 0.8 million Black and 5.4 million white nursing home patients covered by Medicare between 2011 and 2019 to estimate race-specific value-added measures for more than 8,000 nursing homes in the United States. We estimate that the average nursing home value-added experienced by Black patients is about 30% lower than that received by white patients. Most of this gap reflects differences in value-added experienced by similar Black and white patients within the same nursing home, rather than differences in value-added across the nursing homes they go to.

title: Financial Stability Implications of Generative AI: Taming the Animal Spirits

detail.title: Financial Stability Implications of Generative AI: Taming the Animal Spirits

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the adoption of generative AI on financial stability. We conduct laboratory-style experiments using large language models to replicate classic studies on herd behavior in investment decisions. Our results show that AI agents make more rational decisions than humans, relying predominantly on private information over market trends. Increased reliance on AI-powered investment advice could therefore potentially lead to fewer asset price bubbles arising from animal spirits that trade by following the herd. However, exploring variations in the experimental settings reveals that AI agents can be induced to herd optimally when explicitly guided to make profit-maximizing decisions. While optimal herding improves market discipline, this behavior still carries potential implications for financial stability. In other experimental variations, we show that AI agents are not purely algorithmic, but have inherited some elements of human conditioning and bias.

detail.abstract: We use extended fraud alerts in anonymized credit reports to examine how identity theft, and subsequent clean-up, affects consumers’ credit outcomes. The immediate effects of fraud for these consumers are negative, relatively small, and transitory. After placing an alert, these consumers experience persistent declines in delinquencies and a 12-point increase in credit scores, and 11 percent of filers become prime consumers. Many of these consumers take advantage of their improved creditworthiness and obtain additional credit. Although alert filers have larger balances, their performance on loans is as good as better than before fraud, suggestive of a change in behavior following fraud.
